Twenty Third Indian Antarctic Expedition
Ministry of Earth Sciences,  Technical Publication No. 21, pp 83-104
Study of Total Column Ozone and Direct Solar 
Irradiance (UV-B) at Maitri, Antarctica
Pa van S. Kulkarni*t : j : , S.L. Jainf, B.C. Arya1 , Sachin D Ghudef,
Ashok Kumar' and Shahnawaz*
fRadio and Atmospheric Sciences Division, National Physical Laboratory,
New Delhi-110012
^Dept. of Physics and Astrophysics, University of Delhi, Delhi - 110007 
ABSTRACT
During the 16th , 21s t, 22n d  and 23r d  Indian Antarctic expedition conducted in 
1997,2002-03 and 2004 respectively, measurement of columnar ozone and direct UV 
irradiances have been made using MICROTOPS II Sun-photometer from the Indian 
station Maitri (70° 45' S, 11° 44' E). It is found that the ozone hole depth fluctuated 
from year-to-year. The minimum columnar ozone observed over Maitri was 135 
(±9.3) DU, 185 (±12) DU, 126 (±9.7) DU and 159.8 (±8.8) DU during spring 1997, 
2002, 2003 and 2004, respectively. Ozone concentration below 220 DU (nominal 
ozone threshold value) during Antarctic spring (day 225-365) over Maitri has been 
observed to be 45.1 %, 20.7 %, 62.7 % and 60 % in 1997, 2002, 2003 and 2004, 
respectively. The instantaneous irradiances at 305 ± 0.9, 312 ± 0.9 and 320 ± 1  .Onm 
during a no-ozone-hole (13 December 2004) and an ozone-hole (4 October 2004) 
period have been observed to be about 0.031, 0.150 and 0.299Wm22 and 0.010,
0.049 and 0.102Wm22, respectively at local noontime. The observations of the 
direct UV irradiances are compared with tropospheric ultraviolet visible (TUV) 
radiation transfer model calculations. The model estimate shows that, during the 
ozone-hole period, a loss of ozone of the order of 44% leads to an increase in 
irradiance of the order of 410%, 90% and 25% at 305 ± 0.9,312 ± 0.9 and 320 ± 1  .Onm, 
respectively. The relationship between change in UV irradiance due to a change in 
column ozone is obtained using a TUV model and irradiances thus estimated from 
this relationship are found to compare well with the observed irradiances.
Keywords: Antarctica, Ozone hole, UV-B irradiance, TUV model

84 Pavan S. Kulkarni et al.
INTRODUCTION
Total Ozone Column (TOC) is the total amount of ozone present in a 
column extending vertically from Earth’s surface to the top of the 
atmosphere. Stratospheric ozone protects life on the surface of the Earth, 
by screening out genetically destructive ultraviolet radiation from Sun and 
shielding the Earth surface from harmful ultraviolet radiation. Total Ozone 
Column (TOC) is photo-chemically controlled by chemically active species 
in the oxygen, hydrogen, nitrogen, chlorine and bromine families. Most of 
the ozone is produced over the tropics and transported into the polar region 
by the Brewer-Dobson circulation. The total ozone column is decreasing at 
mid latitudes of northern and southern hemisphere (Harris et al, 1997). In 
1985, Farman et al of the British Antarctic Survey first reported the depletion 
of ozone over Antarctica during the southern hemisphere spring period. 
Thereafter, numerous studies based on various ground and satellite 
measurements (Crutzen and Arnold, 1986; Manney et al, 1996; Kondratyev 
and Varotsos, 2000; Johnston, 1971; Farman et al, 1985; Hartmann, 1994; 
Newman, 1986) have shown an overall declining trend of total ozone (TOZ) 
content globally during 1979-94.
The formation of ill-famed ozone hole over Antarctica during Antarctic 
spring is mainly because of catalytic depletion of ozone due to heterogeneous 
chemical reactions which take place on the surface of the polar stratospheric 
cloud (PSCs) (Crutzen and Arnold, 1986; Manney et al, 1996; Kondratyev 
and Varotsos, 2000; Johnston, 1971) inside the polar vortex. Two types of 
PSCs have been discovered, (Crutzen and Arnold, 1986) that provide a 
surface for heterogeneous reactions to take place (Cadle et al, 1975) in the 
presence of sunlight, which enhance the production and lifetime of reactive 
chlorine that convert less reactive molecules into much more reactive forms 
which readily destroy ozone (WMO, 1999).
Ground-based measurements, satellite estimates and model calculations 
of ultraviolet irradiance, particularly in the UV-B range, have recently been 
reported and helped in quantifying effects of solar ultraviolet radiation on 
biological systems (McKinlay and Diffey, 1987; Frederick and Lubin, 1988; 
Cullen et al, 1992; Bais et al, 1993; Zerefos et al, 1995; Bernhard et al, 1997; 
Herman et al, 1996; Katsambas et al, 1997; Minschwaner, 1999; Madronich 
et al, 1998; Feretis et al, 2002; Palancar and Toseli, 2002). The evidence is 
overwhelming that under cloud-free skies UV-B radiation is controlled largely 
by ozone (Bais et al, 1993; Kondratyev et al, 1995; Bodhaine et al, 1997;

Mayer et al, 1997; Taalas et al, 1997; Varotsos et al, 2001). The response of 
UV-B radiation to ozone changes is strongly dependent on wavelength
